title: Context playbook: what people prefer and trust, by product, page and user
how_to_use: Pick the context closest to the page being designed (product x page x user). Use 'styles.preferred' as the starting style family, stay inside 'avoid', and check the design against the listed measures. Evidence ids (E###) point to evidence.jsonl; confidence says how much the evidence carries the advice (high = A/B evidence that fits this context directly; medium = A/B evidence from a neighbouring context or mixed findings; low = mostly C/D or extrapolated). Where evidence is thin, test with users before committing.

global_rules.rule: The first screen is judged in about 50 ms on visual complexity and typicality: keep the first view calm and recognisable for its category; put novelty in details, not structure.
Every interactive element needs a visible signifier (shape, border, shadow or colour that says clickable); flat without signifiers costs scanning time.
Never place text on translucent or busy backgrounds without a solid scrim that keeps WCAG contrast.
Light mode is the default for reading; offer dark mode, and test small text in dark mode especially.
Motion: 100-500 ms, ease-out, animate changes of view not data over time, no parallax or large scroll effects without a reduced-motion path.
Waits: real speed first; then show the next content early, a moderate-speed progress animation, and percent-done for waits over a few seconds.
No dark patterns: visible prices and fees, equal-weight reject and cancel, no trick questions or obstruction; they lift short-term numbers and cost trust.
Colour meaning claims are weak: choose colour for contrast, grouping and consistency, not for psychological effects.
Judge daily tools after repeated use, not first sight; first-impression and preference votes overstate novelty.

contexts.name: RollCall: expert trader's main workspace (dashboard, chart, positions) on desktop

preferred: flat 2.0 / restrained Material with clear signifiers
classical aesthetics (ordered, aligned, grid)
acceptable: dark theme variant for long sessions and dim rooms
styles.why: Experts gain from dense, well-grouped displays and lose speed from novice scaffolding; classical order is the part of beauty that is also usable (E132, E131, E022, E045).

contexts.density: High but grouped: many numbers per view, separated by alignment and spacing between groups; grouping helps experts make fewer errors (E132). Clutter measured, not guessed (E173).
contexts.depth: Minimal: one layer of elevation for panels and menus; signifiers on every control (E055, E057).
contexts.motion: Almost none on data: no animated trends, no confetti; brief transitions only when a view changes (E080, E082, E127).
contexts.colour: Neutral base, one accent; gains and losses by colour plus sign or icon (not colour alone); contrast checked by number (E100, E101).
contexts.type: Tabular figures, 14-16 px minimum for numbers, clear hierarchy by weight; line length irrelevant for tables but labels must be readable (E094, E097).
contexts.imagery: None decorative; charts are the imagery.
avoid: gamified rewards (confetti, badges, streaks) that raise trading volume (E127, E128)
attention lists like 'top movers' as the main entry point (E125, E126)
trust_signals: exact timestamps and data source on every figure
fees and costs visible before any action (E053, E026)
contexts.test_with_users: Owner uses it for a week, then SUS and a task-time check on 5 key tasks (E161, E179); first-click test on new layouts (E184).

contexts.name: RollCall: data tables (watchlists, orders, trade history) for the expert

preferred: plain grid tables, classical order
styles.why: Tables serve find, compare, view-edit and act tasks (E154); grouping dense data helps (E132).

contexts.density: Compact rows by default with a density toggle; zebra or row separators, right-aligned numbers (E132, E154).
contexts.depth: Flat rows; sticky header and first column for orientation.
contexts.motion: Highlight a changed value briefly (under 500 ms) and settle; no continuous flashing (E088, E093).
contexts.colour: Colour only for state (gain/loss/alert) and always with a second cue (E100).
contexts.type: Monospaced or tabular numerals; readable identifier in the first column (E154).
avoid: hiding columns behind hover-only menus (E114, E115)
animated reordering while the user reads
trust_signals: sort and filter state always visible
contexts.test_with_users: Find and compare tasks timed with the owner; five-user rounds for new layouts (E181).

contexts.name: RollCall: learner's first run and onboarding

preferred: friendly flat 2.0 with warm accents and real explanations
styles.why: Warm design helps learning and motivation (E134); novices need guidance that experts do not (E131).

contexts.density: Low: one idea per screen, generous spacing; progressive disclosure toward the expert view (E131, E133).
contexts.depth: Clear cards and buttons with obvious signifiers (E055).
contexts.motion: Short transitions that show where things go; nothing celebratory around trades (E127, E082).
contexts.colour: Warm, friendly accents allowed on learning content, not on trade actions (E134, E127).
avoid: price-trend push notifications by default for beginners (E129)
trust_signals: plain-language risk and fee disclosure up front (E053)
who runs the service and how to reach them (E026)
contexts.test_with_users: Five learners per round, three rounds (E182); comprehension checks, not only liking; desirability words (E183).

contexts.name: RollCall: lessons and explanations for learners

preferred: editorial reading layout with warm, friendly graphics
styles.why: Pleasant colours and friendly faces in learning graphics raise comprehension and transfer (E134, E135); people scan, so structure must carry meaning (E141, E142).

contexts.density: Low to medium; headings, bullets, bold key terms (E142).
contexts.depth: Flat content; interactive examples with clear affordances.
contexts.motion: Animated transitions to explain changes in a chart are fine (E082); avoid animated data playback for analysis (E080).
contexts.type: 18 px or larger body for long text (E094); line length controlled (E097).
contexts.imagery: Diagrams and real examples; faces in learning graphics can help (E134).
contexts.test_with_users: Comprehension quiz after reading; five-user think-aloud rounds (E182).

contexts.name: RollCall: order entry and confirmation (any user)

preferred: plain, high-contrast form with one primary action
styles.why: Form guidelines make forms faster and more satisfying (E145); costs hidden until late drive abandonment and distrust (E146, E053).

contexts.density: Only needed fields (E147); review step shows every cost.
contexts.depth: Primary button solid, secondary outlined; clear focus states.
contexts.motion: Instant feedback (under 0.1 s) on submit, then status (E085).
contexts.colour: No celebratory colour after a trade (E127).
avoid: confetti or reward animations after trades (E127, E128)
trust_signals: total cost and risk shown before confirm (E053, E146)
undo or cancel window where possible
contexts.test_with_users: Error-rate and time on scripted orders; first-click test (E184).

contexts.name: RollCall: mobile check-ins (positions, alerts) on the go

preferred: platform-native flat 2.0 / Material, bottom tab bar
acceptable: expressive emphasis on the one key action (E166)
styles.why: Attention on the move comes in seconds-long bursts (E113); most people use one hand (E108); hidden navigation is slower (E115).

contexts.density: One glanceable summary per screen; details one tap away.
contexts.depth: Bottom sheets and cards with clear signifiers.
contexts.motion: Minimal; no motion that encourages impulsive trades.
avoid: targets under about 9 mm / 44 px (E110, E111, E123)
one-tap trading from notifications; phones increase lottery-like buying (E130)
contexts.test_with_users: One-handed task tests on the owner's phone; reach checked against thumb model (E109).

contexts.name: Temper: developer console (workflow runs, logs, agent graphs)

preferred: restrained flat 2.0, classical grid, light and dark themes
acceptable: dark default if users ask; test small text in dark (E061)
styles.why: Expert tools favour dense, grouped information and shortcuts (E132, E133); dashboards must be designed for their genre (E143, E144).

contexts.density: High, grouped; monitoring vs analysis views separated (E143, E144).
contexts.motion: Status changes animated briefly; streaming logs without flashing (E088, E093).
contexts.colour: Status colours plus icons; neutral base (E100).
contexts.type: Monospace for logs and ids, 13-14 px minimum in dark mode, larger in light (E061).
trust_signals: clear errors with cause and next step
contexts.test_with_users: Five developer tasks per round, keyboard-shortcut discoverability (E133, E181).

contexts.name: Temper: AI agent output, review and correction screens

preferred: plain document-like layout, clear provenance blocks
styles.why: AI guidelines: say what the AI can do and how well, make correction efficient, explain (E137); confidence displays help calibrate trust (E138).

contexts.density: Medium; result first, evidence one click away.
contexts.depth: Distinguish AI-generated content from human-verified with a consistent container style.
contexts.motion: Streaming text is fine; no fake typing delays (E087).
contexts.colour: One colour for AI uncertainty or warnings, consistent.
avoid: human-like persona naming on complex tasks (E051, E052)
contexts.test_with_users: Owner review sessions; measure correction time and trust calibration, not liking.

contexts.name: Temper: marketing and landing pages for a developer audience

preferred: typical SaaS/dev-tool layout with one expressive accent (MAYA)
editorial / Swiss type-led layout
acceptable: dark hero if text contrast holds
styles.why: Typical-for-category pages win first impressions (E002) and novelty must sit in a familiar frame (E025); content predicts return visits (E014).

contexts.density: Low to medium above the fold; real product screenshots and code examples (E072).
contexts.depth: Light: subtle elevation for product shots.
contexts.motion: Small, purposeful; no scroll-jacking or parallax (E090, E091).
contexts.colour: Brand accent on a neutral base.
contexts.imagery: Real product UI and real code, not abstract 3D or stock (E072, E073).
trust_signals: who builds it, docs, pricing visible (E026, E053)
contexts.test_with_users: Five-second test for the message, first-click test on the main CTA, reaction cards (E183, E184).

contexts.name: Marketing and landing pages (consumer or business)

preferred: minimalism with clear hierarchy
flat 2.0
editorial
acceptable: expressive accents, bold colour for younger audiences (E165)
styles.why: Appeal and trust are judged in 50 ms (E001, E015); low complexity and typicality win (E002); design look is the most-cited credibility cue (E027).

contexts.density: Low above the fold; most attention stays in the first two screens (E118).
contexts.colour: Contrast-led; don't rely on colour psychology (E101).
contexts.imagery: Real people and real product; faces raise warmth (E029, E073).
avoid: dark patterns and fake urgency (E035, E039)
trust_signals: contact details, real team, clear pricing (E026, E053)
contexts.test_with_users: Five-second and first-click tests; A/B only on real traffic after novelty fades (E163, E184).

contexts.name: SaaS and B2B apps: settings, admin and forms

preferred: flat 2.0 / Material with standard patterns
styles.why: Pattern-breaking expressive concepts tested worse (E167); form guidelines speed completion (E145).

contexts.density: Medium; group related settings; labels above fields (E145).
contexts.test_with_users: Task success and SUS after tasks (E179).

contexts.name: Empty states in any app

preferred: product's own style; one clear next action
styles.why: Empty states teach and lead to the key task (E153); intentional space is fine but must not look broken (E104).

contexts.density: Low, but intentional: explanation plus one action.
contexts.imagery: Optional small illustration; informative beats decorative (E072).
trust_signals: say why it is empty and what will appear
contexts.test_with_users: First-click test on the empty state (E184).

contexts.name: E-commerce product pages and checkout

preferred: clean flat 2.0, product photography first
styles.why: Abandonment comes from extra costs, trust and forced accounts (E146); checkout should have 12-14 fields (E147).

contexts.density: Product page rich in information; checkout minimal (E147).
contexts.depth: Clear buttons; trust badges near payment.
contexts.imagery: Informative product photos and real people; decorative stock ignored (E072, E029).
avoid: hidden costs and dark patterns (E031, E032)
trust_signals: total price early, guest checkout, returns policy (E146, E053)
contexts.test_with_users: Checkout usability rounds; Baymard-style field count (E147).

contexts.name: Health information and services

preferred: calm classical layout, clear authority signals
styles.why: Poor design gets health sites rejected fast; credibility and authority decide trust; ads lower it (E028, E136).

contexts.density: Low to medium; plain language.
contexts.type: Large body for older readers (E098, E151).
contexts.imagery: Real clinicians and patients over stock (E073).
trust_signals: author credentials, review dates, owner of the site (E136, E026)
contexts.test_with_users: Include older and low-vision users (E151).

contexts.name: News, editorial and long reading

preferred: editorial / Swiss typographic layout
acceptable: dark reading mode as an option
styles.why: People read 20-28% of words and scan; formatting prevents F-pattern loss (E141, E142); multimedia did not raise credibility (E157).

contexts.density: Medium; clear headings and summaries.
contexts.colour: Light background for long reading (E060, E061).
contexts.test_with_users: Comprehension and scanning tests.

contexts.name: Education and children's products

preferred: warm, colourful, illustrated, age-specific
styles.why: Warm design boosts learning and motivation, most for children (E134, E135); children need age-narrow design (E150); teens hate clutter (E149).

contexts.density: Low; big targets.
contexts.depth: Obvious, physical-looking buttons for young children (E066 shows skeuomorphic cues help less experienced users).
contexts.type: Large; few words for young children.
contexts.test_with_users: Test by age band (E150).

contexts.name: Government and public services

preferred: plain classical (GOV.UK-like)
styles.why: Accessibility over elegance (E155); older users need contrast and large targets (E151); forms guidelines (E145).

contexts.density: One thing per page.
contexts.test_with_users: Include access needs and older adults (E151).

contexts.name: Luxury and fashion brands

preferred: minimal, generous white space, editorial photography
styles.why: White space carries prestige meaning (E159); some luxury shoppers see e-commerce tools as cheapening (E158).

contexts.density: Low, intentional space.
avoid: low contrast thin type for body (E060)
contexts.test_with_users: Reaction cards for brand words (E183).

contexts.name: Portfolios and agencies

preferred: expressive, brutalist or editorial as a statement
styles.why: Expressive aesthetics signal originality (E046); brutalism can work, anti-design rarely (E071); showcase taste differs from users' (E169).

contexts.density: Varies by concept.
avoid: motion that cannot be turned off (E093)
contexts.test_with_users: Five-second test for the intended impression.

contexts.name: Social, video and entertainment feeds

preferred: expressive Material / bold colour for young audiences
styles.why: Young users prefer expressive design (E165); autoplay and recommendations reduce agency (E139).

contexts.density: Medium; media first.
trust_signals: clear controls over what is shown
contexts.test_with_users: Agency and satisfaction measures, not only time spent (E139).

contexts.name: Any product with many older users (45+)

preferred: clear, colourful-enough, flat 2.0 with strong signifiers
styles.why: Older users do not want plainer (E008, E009) but need large text, contrast and big targets (E151, E098).

contexts.density: Medium; no clutter.
contexts.test_with_users: Recruit 45+ users; SUS after tasks (E179).

contexts.name: Games and game-like interfaces

preferred: genre-typical style; expressive allowed
styles.why: Removing the HUD raised expert immersion; the right interface depends on expertise (E156); expertise reversal (E131).

contexts.density: Adjustable by expertise.
avoid: fixed dense HUD for all players
contexts.test_with_users: Playtests by expertise level.

evidence_note: Evidence entries cited by this playbook, from the Design research base (~/design-lab/research/ui-preferences/evidence.jsonl, 184 claims). Grades: A peer-reviewed large/replicated, B peer-reviewed single study or large rigorous industry research, C industry/vendor research, D opinion and guidance. A and B quotes were re-checked against their sources on 2026-10-04.

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: People judge a web page's visual appeal within about 50 ms, and 50 ms ratings agree closely with 500 ms ratings: the first screen's look is judged before anything is read.
evidence.source: Lindgaard, Fernandes, Dudek & Brown 2006, Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression!
evidence.authors: Lindgaard G, Fernandes G, Dudek C, Brown J
evidence.sample_size: 3 lab studies (participant counts not in abstract); repeated ratings of web home pages
evidence.method: lab experiments, 500 ms and 50 ms exposures, repeated visual-appeal ratings
evidence.quote_or_number: visual appeal can be assessed within 50 ms, suggesting that web designers have about 50 ms to make a good first impression

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: Visual complexity and prototypicality shape aesthetic ratings within the first 50 ms; pages with low visual complexity that look like a typical site of their kind are rated most appealing.
evidence.source: Tuch, Presslaber, Stöcklin, Opwis & Bargas-Avila 2012, The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites
evidence.authors: Tuch AN, Presslaber EE, Stöcklin M, Opwis K, Bargas-Avila JA
evidence.sample_size: Study 1 n = 59 lab participants rating 119 real website screenshots (plus 267 online raters for stimulus selection); Study 2 at 17-50 ms
evidence.method: two lab experiments, presentation time 17-1000 ms, low/medium/high complexity x low/high prototypicality
evidence.quote_or_number: websites with low VC and high PT were perceived as highly appealing

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: High visual complexity costs the most appeal; low and medium complexity are liked about equally, so the 'inverted U' (moderate is best) is weak: the rule is avoid busy, not avoid simple.
evidence.source: Reinecke et al. 2013, Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics (CHI 2013)
evidence.authors: Reinecke K, Yeh T, Miratrix L, Mardiko R, Zhao Y, Liu J, Gajos KZ
evidence.method: online ratings after 500 ms exposure, mixed-effects regression with quadratic terms
evidence.quote_or_number: a high visual complexity results in the largest decrease in appeal, but websites with low levels of complexity are similarly liked to those with a medium complexity

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: In the 40,000-person LabintheWild data, older people preferred more visual complexity, not less; people aged 12-40 did not differ much.
evidence.source: Reinecke & Gajos 2014, Quantifying visual preferences around the world
evidence.method: online volunteer study, peak-appeal estimates per age group
evidence.quote_or_number: The older someone is, the more complex they prefer websites to be.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Older participants found plain, colourless websites less appealing than any other age group did.
evidence.source: Reinecke & Gajos 2014, Quantifying visual preferences around the world
evidence.quote_or_number: older participants find plain, colorless websites less visually appealing than any other age group

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: Users say content matters most; aesthetics drives the first impression, but only content predicted intention to revisit or recommend (aesthetics added only a small effect in a replication).
evidence.source: Thielsch, Blotenberg & Jaron 2014, User evaluation of websites: From first impression to recommendation
evidence.authors: Thielsch MT, Blotenberg I, Jaron R
evidence.sample_size: Study 1 n = 330; Study 2 n = 300 (4 websites); Study 3 n = 512 (42 websites)
evidence.method: surveys and path models across use phases, replicated
evidence.quote_or_number: aesthetics had the largest influence on first impressions, while all three constructs had an impact on first and overall impressions. However, only content contributed significantly to the intention to revisit or recommend a website

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Judgements of trustworthiness and usability made from a 50 ms glimpse of a home page are largely driven by its visual appeal.
evidence.source: Lindgaard, Dudek, Sen, Sumegi & Noonan 2011, An exploration of relations between visual appeal, trustworthiness and perceived usability of homepages
evidence.authors: Lindgaard G, Dudek C, Sen D, Sumegi L, Noonan P
evidence.sample_size: 3 experiments (counts not in abstract), 50 ms exposures
evidence.method: lab experiments, within- and between-subject designs with masking
evidence.quote_or_number: all three types of judgments are largely driven by visual appeal

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: Over seven weeks of real use (110 people, a coffee machine), visual aesthetics had no effect on user experience, including perceived usability: the beauty effect can fade with repeated use.
evidence.source: Sauer & Sonderegger 2022, Visual aesthetics and user experience: A multiple-session experiment
evidence.method: longitudinal lab experiment, 2x2x7 mixed design (aesthetics x usability x session)
evidence.quote_or_number: We found no effect of visual aesthetics on user experience (including perceived usability as the chief outcome variable)

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: Visual clarity (order, alignment, low complexity) explains much of why people who find an interface beautiful also find it usable.
evidence.source: Schrepp, Otten, Blum & Thomaschewski 2021, What causes the dependency between perceived aesthetics and perceived usability?
evidence.authors: Schrepp M, Otten R, Blum K, Thomaschewski J
evidence.venue: International Journal of Interactive Multimedia and Artificial Intelligence 6(6)
evidence.sample_size: two large online studies (counts not in abstract)
evidence.method: survey studies with mediation analysis; new UEQ+ visual clarity scale
evidence.quote_or_number: We present two large studies that show a strong mediator effect of visual clarity on the dependency between perceived aesthetics and perceived usability

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: Most advanced, yet acceptable (MAYA): typicality and novelty both raise aesthetic preference, but they suppress each other, so the best designs are new within a familiar frame.
evidence.source: Hekkert, Snelders & van Wieringen 2003, 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
evidence.authors: Hekkert P, Snelders D, van Wieringen PCW
evidence.sample_size: 3 studies of consumer products (counts not in abstract)
evidence.method: rating studies of typicality, novelty and preference with partial correlations
evidence.quote_or_number: typicality (operationalized as 'goodness of example') and novelty are jointly and equally effective in explaining the aesthetic preference of consumer products, but that they suppress each other's effect

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: In a 1,400-person US/European study of 51 site elements, credibility rose most with a 'real-world feel' (address, people, organisation), ease of use, visible expertise, trustworthiness and tailoring; commercial pushiness and amateurism hurt it.
evidence.source: Fogg, Marshall, Laraki, Osipovich, Varma, Fang, Paul & Rangnekar 2001, What makes Web sites credible? A report on a large quantitative study
evidence.authors: Fogg BJ, Marshall J, Laraki O, Osipovich A, Varma C, Fang N, Paul J, Rangnekar A
evidence.sample_size: over 1,400 participants (US and Europe), 51 site elements
evidence.method: online survey rating how each element affects credibility; factor analysis
evidence.quote_or_number: The two types of elements that hurt credibility were "commercial implications" and "amateurism"

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: When 2,684 people judged live sites' credibility, the site's visual 'design look' was the thing they mentioned most (46% of comments), ahead of information structure and focus.
evidence.source: Fogg, Soohoo, Danielson, Marable, Stanford & Tauber 2003, How do users evaluate the credibility of Web sites? A study with over 2,500 participants
evidence.authors: Fogg BJ, Soohoo C, Danielson DR, Marable L, Stanford J, Tauber ER
evidence.method: online study, paired live sites, coded free-text comments
evidence.quote_or_number: of the site was mentioned most frequently, being present in 46.1% of the comments

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: On health sites, poor design appeal made people reject a site quickly (mistrust), while the credibility of the information and personalised content decided which sites they kept and trusted.
evidence.source: Sillence, Briggs, Fishwick & Harris 2004, Trust and mistrust of online health sites
evidence.authors: Sillence E, Briggs P, Fishwick L, Harris P
evidence.sample_size: 15 women facing a risky health decision, 4 weekly sessions
evidence.method: observed searching, think-aloud and group discussion, content analysis
evidence.quote_or_number: design appeal predicted rejection (mistrust) and credibility of information and personalisation of content predicted selection (trust)

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Photos of people with visible faces made shopping sites feel more appealing and warmer (social presence), which in turn raised trust; the images did not raise trust directly.
evidence.source: Cyr, Head, Larios & Pan 2009, Exploring human images in website design: a multi-method approach
evidence.authors: Cyr D, Head M, Larios H, Pan B
evidence.sample_size: controlled experiment in Canada, Germany and Japan (count not in abstract)
evidence.method: experiment with questionnaire, interviews and eye tracking; 3 image conditions
evidence.quote_or_number: All expected relationships in the model were supported except no direct relationship was found between the human image conditions and trust

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Dark patterns are common: a crawl of about 11,000 shopping sites found 1,818 instances of 15 types, 183 sites using outright deception, and 22 vendors selling them as ready-made features.
evidence.source: Mathur, Acar, Friedman, Lucherini, Mayer, Chetty & Narayanan 2019, Dark patterns at scale: findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites
evidence.authors: Mathur A, Acar G, Friedman MJ, Lucherini E, Mayer J, Chetty M, Narayanan A
evidence.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 3 (CSCW)
evidence.sample_size: about 53,000 product pages from about 11,000 shopping sites
evidence.quote_or_number: Analyzing ~53K product pages from ~11K shopping websites, we discover 1,818 dark pattern instances, together representing 15 types and 7 broader categories

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Dark patterns work: in representative US samples, mild dark patterns more than doubled sign-ups for a dubious service and aggressive ones nearly quadrupled them.
evidence.source: Luguri & Strahilevitz 2021, Shining a light on dark patterns
evidence.sample_size: two large-scale experiments with representative samples of US consumers
evidence.quote_or_number: users exposed to mild dark patterns were more than twice as likely to sign up for a dubious service as those assigned to the control group, and users in the aggressive dark pattern condition were almost four times as likely to subscribe

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Aggressive dark patterns caused a strong backlash in mood toward the company; mild ones did not, which is why mild manipulation persists unnoticed.
evidence.source: Luguri & Strahilevitz 2021, Shining a light on dark patterns
evidence.method: randomised online experiments with mood measures
evidence.quote_or_number: whereas aggressive dark patterns generated a powerful backlash among consumers, mild dark patterns did not

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: The most effective manipulations were hidden information, trick questions and obstruction; 'act now' urgency messages did not increase purchases of a costly service.
evidence.source: Luguri & Strahilevitz 2021, Shining a light on dark patterns
evidence.quote_or_number: Hidden information, trick question, and obstruction strategies were particularly likely to manipulate consumers successfully

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: 95% of 240 popular mobile apps contained at least one dark pattern (seven types on average), and most of 589 users did not recognise them unless told what to look for.
evidence.source: Di Geronimo, Braz, Fregnan, Palomba & Bacchelli 2020, UI dark patterns and where to find them: a study on mobile applications and user perception
evidence.authors: Di Geronimo L, Braz L, Fregnan E, Palomba F, Bacchelli A
evidence.method: expert app analysis plus online perception experiment
evidence.quote_or_number: 95% of the analyzed apps contain one or more forms of Dark Patterns

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Consent pop-up design changes choices a lot: removing 'reject' from the first layer raised consent by 22-23 points; only 11.8% of popular UK consent pop-ups met minimal legal requirements.
evidence.source: Nouwens, Liccardi, Veale, Karger & Kagal 2020, Dark patterns after the GDPR: scraping consent pop-ups and demonstrating their influence
evidence.authors: Nouwens M, Liccardi I, Veale M, Karger D, Kagal L
evidence.sample_size: 680 consent designs scraped from top 10,000 UK sites; field experiment with 40 participants
evidence.quote_or_number: removing the opt-out button from the first page increases consent by 22-23 percentage points

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: People know dark patterns exist, but knowing does not help them resist; younger people spot them more often yet are unsure of the harm.
evidence.source: Bongard-Blanchy, Rossi, Rivas, Doublet, Koenig & Lenzini 2021, 'I am definitely manipulated, even when I am aware of it. It's ridiculous!' Dark patterns from the end-user perspective
evidence.authors: Bongard-Blanchy K, Rossi A, Rivas S, Doublet S, Koenig V, Lenzini G
evidence.quote_or_number: being aware does not equip users with the ability to oppose such influence

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: A shop built with five dark patterns annoyed shoppers more, and annoyance went with lower trust in the brand.
evidence.source: Voigt, Schlögl & Groth 2021, Dark patterns in online shopping: of sneaky tricks, perceived annoyance and respective brand trust
evidence.authors: Voigt C, Schlögl S, Groth A
evidence.method: between-subject experiment-based survey with two versions of a fictitious shop
evidence.quote_or_number: Results show a higher level of perceived annoyance with those who used the dark pattern version of the online shop

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: For online banking, visual design factors (title, menu, main image, colour) can be deliberately tuned to raise felt trustworthiness.
evidence.source: Kim & Moon 1998, Designing towards emotional usability in customer interfaces: trustworthiness of cyber-banking system interfaces
evidence.sample_size: four studies with Korean bank staff, developers and customers (late teens to early forties)
evidence.method: emotion scale development, design-factor correlation, two designed interfaces
evidence.quote_or_number: it is possible to manipulate the visual design factors of the customer interface in order to induce a target emotion, such as trustworthiness

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.claim: People judge website looks on two separate dimensions: classical aesthetics (orderly, clear, clean, symmetrical, close to usability rules) and expressive aesthetics (creative, original, fascinating, special effects, convention-breaking).
evidence.source: Lavie & Tractinsky 2004, Assessing dimensions of perceived visual aesthetics of web sites
evidence.sample_size: four studies (Study 1 n = 125 engineering students; confirmatory sample n = 192 plus hold-out)
evidence.method: exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of adjective ratings
evidence.quote_or_number: These notions emphasize orderly and clear design and are closely related to many of the design rules advocated by usability experts

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Expressive aesthetics is the designer's creativity and originality, including the ability to break conventions; it is distinguishable from classical clarity and is what gives a design character.
evidence.source: Lavie & Tractinsky 2004, Assessing dimensions of perceived visual aesthetics of web sites
evidence.quote_or_number: The expressive aesthetics dimension is manifested by the designers' creativity and originality and by the ability to break design conventions

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Investors relied more on an unnamed robo-advisor than a named one; giving an algorithm a human name backfired when the task looked complex.
evidence.source: Hodge, Mendoza & Sinha 2021, The effect of humanizing robo-advisors on investor judgments
evidence.authors: Hodge FD, Mendoza KI, Sinha RK
evidence.quote_or_number: investors are more likely to rely on the investment recommendation of an unnamed robo-advisor

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: A robo-advisor reduced investors' disposition effect, but adding human-like social design (a name, chat language) made decisions worse because people asked it for advice less.
evidence.source: Back, Morana & Spann 2023, When do robo-advisors make us better investors? The impact of social design elements on investor behavior
evidence.authors: Back C, Morana S, Spann M
evidence.venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics 103
evidence.sample_size: two consequential induced-value experiments (counts not in abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: imbuing the robo-advisor with social design elements (e.g., a name and the ability to communicate using natural language) negatively affects investment behavior

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: NN/g's Singapore study found the same four trust factors across Western and Asian users as Nielsen listed in 1999: design quality, up-front disclosure (prices, fees, policies before sign-up), comprehensive current content, and links to the rest of the web.
evidence.source: Harley 2016, Trustworthiness in web design: 4 credibility factors (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: qualitative usability study in Singapore (count not stated)
evidence.quote_or_number: In our study, we observed that these very same factors continue to influence users.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: In a 71-person eyetracking experiment on 9 page pairs, pages whose clickable elements had weak (flat) signifiers took 22% longer to scan than the same pages with strong signifiers.
evidence.source: Moran 2017, Flat UI elements attract less attention and cause uncertainty (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: 71 general web users, 9 page pairs, between-subjects
evidence.method: quantitative eyetracking experiment, fixations and time to find the target
evidence.quote_or_number: On average participants spent 22% more time (i.e., slower task performance) looking at the pages with weak signifiers.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: The same eyetracking study found 25% more fixations on weak-signifier pages, meaning more searching before people found what to click.
evidence.source: Moran 2017, Flat UI elements attract less attention and cause uncertainty (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: On average, people had 25% more fixations on the pages with weak signifiers.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: 'Flat 2.0' (mostly flat with subtle shadows, highlights and layers) is recommended over pure flat because it restores depth cues that tell people what can be clicked.
evidence.source: Moran 2015, Flat design: its origins, its problems, and why flat 2.0 is better for users (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: This design style is mostly flat, but it makes use of subtle shadows, highlights, and layers to create some depth in the UI.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Review of the research: people with normal vision read and see detail better in light mode; some people with cataracts and similar conditions may do better in dark mode.
evidence.source: Budiu 2020, Dark mode vs. light mode: which is better? (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: In people with normal vision (or corrected-to-normal vision), visual performance tends to be better with light mode, whereas some people with cataract and related disorders may perform better with dark mode.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Dark text on a light background beat light-on-dark for both younger (18-33) and older (60-85) adults in acuity and proofreading; the authors recommend positive polarity for all ages.
evidence.source: Piepenbrock, Mayr, Mund & Buchner 2013, Positive display polarity is advantageous for both younger and older adults
evidence.authors: Piepenbrock C, Mayr S, Mund I, Buchner A
evidence.sample_size: younger (18-33) and older (60-85) adults (counts not in abstract)
evidence.method: lab experiment, visual acuity test and proofreading in each polarity
evidence.quote_or_number: A positive polarity advantage was found for both age groups. The presentation in positive polarity is recommended for all ages.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: The light-mode reading advantage grows as text gets smaller, so small text on dark backgrounds is the worst case.
evidence.source: Piepenbrock, Mayr & Buchner 2014, Positive display polarity is particularly advantageous for small character sizes
evidence.authors: Piepenbrock C, Mayr S, Buchner A
evidence.sample_size: lab sample (count not in abstract), 4 character sizes 8-14 pt
evidence.quote_or_number: the positive polarity advantage linearly increased with decreasing character size

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: At night with a dim screen, reading in dark mode reduced measured eye fatigue (blink rate, pupil), yet people still preferred light mode out of habit; everyone preferred higher text contrast.
evidence.source: Xie, Song, Liu, Wang & Yu 2021, Study on the effects of display color mode and luminance contrast on visual fatigue
evidence.authors: Xie X, Song F, Liu Y, Wang S, Yu D
evidence.sample_size: lab sample (count not in abstract), 2 x 6 design
evidence.method: lab experiment at low ambient light with eye tracking and rating scales
evidence.quote_or_number: Results showed that reading in the dark mode reduced visual fatigue, as reflected by an increase in blink rate and pupil accommodation.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Older adults (15, interviewed and tested on banking prototypes) preferred a flat online-banking design to a skeuomorphic one, although the skeuomorphic one helped them more than it helped younger adults.
evidence.source: Ellis & Marshall 2019, Can skeuomorphic design provide a better online banking user experience for older adults?
evidence.sample_size: 15 older adults plus 17 younger adults (20-25) as validation
evidence.method: interviews, prototype tests with SUS, observation
evidence.quote_or_number: Results of the experiments showed that our older users preferred the flat prototype to the skeuomorphic one

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Apple's Liquid Glass (iOS 26) was criticised by NN/g for obscuring content: translucent controls over busy backgrounds lower text contrast, and floating controls crowd and shrink tap targets.
evidence.source: Budiu 2025, Liquid Glass is cracked, and usability suffers in iOS 26 (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: iOS 26's visual language obscures content instead of letting it take the spotlight.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Text placed over images or translucent layers is a long-known contrast problem; Liquid Glass makes it routine.
evidence.source: Budiu 2025, Liquid Glass is cracked, and usability suffers in iOS 26 (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Text on top of images is a bad idea because the contrast between the text and the background is often too low.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Brutalism (raw, deliberately plain) can work in visual design, but anti-design (deliberately chaotic, convention-breaking) should be avoided for most products.
evidence.source: Moran 2017, Brutalism and antidesign (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Brutalism can be used effectively in visual design, but antidesign should be avoided for most products.

evidence.question: Q4
evidence.claim: Eyetracking shows people study photos that carry information (products, real people) and ignore decorative feel-good images.
evidence.source: Nielsen 2010 (reviewed 2026), Photos as web content (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Users pay close attention to photos and other images that contain relevant information but ignore fluffy pictures used to "jazz up" web pages.

evidence.question: Q7
evidence.claim: Users ignore stock photos of generic people but look at photos of real people who actually work at the company.
evidence.source: Nielsen 2010 (reviewed 2026), Photos as web content (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: users ignore stock photos of generic people

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Progress bars with animated ribbing that moves backwards and slows down made the same wait feel 11% shorter than a plain solid bar.
evidence.source: Harrison, Yeo & Hudson 2010, Faster progress bars: manipulating perceived duration with visual augmentations
evidence.authors: Harrison C, Yeo Z, Hudson SE
evidence.sample_size: lab participants (count not in abstract), series of paired comparisons
evidence.method: lab experiments, paired comparisons of progress-bar designs and duration judgements
evidence.quote_or_number: showed that it reduces the perceived duration among our participants by 11%

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: In animated transitions on a phone, showing the next screen's content earlier mattered more for feeling fast than any other transition variable tested.
evidence.source: Huhtala, Sarjanoja, Mäntyjärvi, Isomursu & Häkkilä 2010, Animated UI transitions and perception of time: a user study on animated effects on a mobile screen
evidence.authors: Huhtala J, Sarjanoja AH, Mäntyjärvi J, Isomursu M, Häkkilä J
evidence.method: lab user study of transition variants
evidence.quote_or_number: bringing up the next image earlier dominates the perception of a fast transition over other variables examined in the study

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Across several experiments, moderate-speed wait animations made waits feel shortest, compared with no animation, slow or fast animation (a U-shaped, not linear, effect).
evidence.source: Ding & Kyung 2025, Optimizing animation speed: convex effects on perceived waiting time and digital customer experience
evidence.sample_size: multiple experiments (1a-6) incl. field tests (counts not in abstract)
evidence.method: series of lab and field experiments
evidence.quote_or_number: moderate-speed animations minimize perceived waiting time compared to no, slow-moving, or fast-moving animations (experiments 1a-1c)

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: For analysing trends, animated charts were the slowest and least accurate; static traces and small multiples were significantly faster, and small multiples most accurate.
evidence.source: Robertson, Fernandez, Fisher, Lee & Stasko 2008, Effectiveness of animation in trend visualization
evidence.authors: Robertson G, Fernandez R, Fisher D, Lee B, Stasko J
evidence.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics 14(6)
evidence.method: controlled experiment, three trend visualisations x analysis and presentation tasks
evidence.quote_or_number: Animation is the least effective form for analysis; both static depictions of trends are significantly faster than animation, and the small multiples display is more accurate.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Well-designed animated transitions between chart states (e.g. bar to pie, re-sorting) significantly improved people's ability to follow what changed.
evidence.source: Heer & Robertson 2007, Animated transitions in statistical data graphics
evidence.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics 13(6)
evidence.sample_size: two controlled experiments (counts not in abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: finding that animated transitions can significantly improve graphical perception

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Feedback while waiting makes web users willing to wait longer; without it, the tolerable wait for retrieving information is about 2 seconds.
evidence.source: Nah 2004, A study on tolerable waiting time: how long are Web users willing to wait?
evidence.method: lab experiment with feedback vs no feedback
evidence.quote_or_number: the presence of feedback prolongs Web users' tolerable waiting time and the tolerable waiting time for information retrieval is approximately 2 s

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Classic response-time limits: about 0.1 s feels instant, about 1 s keeps the flow of thought, about 10 s is the limit of attention.
evidence.source: Nielsen 1993, Response times: the 3 important limits (Nielsen Norman Group, from Usability Engineering)
evidence.sample_size: n/a (synthesis of Miller 1968, Card et al. 1991)
evidence.quote_or_number: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Use a progress indicator for anything over about 1 second; looping spinners only for short waits, percent-done bars for long ones.
evidence.source: Sherwin 2014, Progress indicators make a slow system less insufferable (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.method: expert guidance citing a University of Nebraska-Lincoln study
evidence.quote_or_number: Use a progress indicator for any action that takes longer than about 1.0 second.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: In a large Yahoo search log, of two identical result pages people clicked more on the one served faster; in a lab study, users of a fast system noticed added delays more than users of a slow one.
evidence.source: Arapakis, Bai & Cambazoglu 2014, Impact of response latency on user behavior in web search
evidence.authors: Arapakis I, Bai X, Cambazoglu BB
evidence.sample_size: controlled user study plus large-scale Yahoo query log
evidence.quote_or_number: given two content-wise identical search result pages, we show that the users are more likely to perform clicks on the result page that is served with lower latency

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Most UI animations should last 100-500 ms: about 100 ms for simple feedback (toggles, checkboxes), 200-300 ms for larger moves; at 500 ms they start to feel like a drag.
evidence.source: Laubheimer 2020, Executing UX animations: duration and motion characteristics (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: In general, the duration of most animations should be in the range of 100-500 ms, depending on complexity and on how far the element is traveling.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Ease-out curves (fast start, gentle stop) make UI motion feel responsive; linear motion looks unnatural.
evidence.source: Laubheimer 2020, Executing UX animations: duration and motion characteristics (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Most frequently, you'll want to use an ease-out animation, that starts quickly but slows down.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: With 86 students, a parallax-scrolling site was rated more fun than the same site without parallax, but not better on usability, satisfaction or visual appeal.
evidence.source: Frederick, Mohler, Vorvoreanu & Glotzbach 2015, The effects of parallax scrolling on user experience in web design
evidence.authors: Frederick DM, Mohler JL, Vorvoreanu M, Glotzbach RJ
evidence.quote_or_number: Participants believed that the parallax scrolling website was more fun than the non-parallax scrolling website.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Two of the 43 people using the parallax site got motion sickness and had significant usability problems.
evidence.source: Frederick, Mohler, Vorvoreanu & Glotzbach 2015, The effects of parallax scrolling on user experience in web design
evidence.authors: Frederick DM, Mohler JL, Vorvoreanu M, Glotzbach RJ
evidence.quote_or_number: two of the participants suffered motion sickness and experienced significant usability issues while interacting with the parallax scrolling website

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: In a US national health survey (n=5,086), 35.4% of adults aged 40+ had measurable vestibular (balance) dysfunction, rising with age.
evidence.source: Agrawal, Carey, Della Santina, Schubert & Minor 2009, Disorders of balance and vestibular function in US adults (NHANES 2001-2004)
evidence.authors: Agrawal Y, Carey JP, Della Santina CC, Schubert MC, Minor LB
evidence.method: national cross-sectional survey with a balance test
evidence.quote_or_number: 35.4% of US adults aged 40 years and older (69 million Americans) had vestibular dysfunction

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.3.3 (AAA): motion triggered by interaction must be possible to turn off unless it is essential.
evidence.source: W3C 2023, Understanding SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (WCAG 2.2)
evidence.quote_or_number: Motion animation triggered by interaction can be disabled, unless the animation is essential to the functionality or the information being conveyed.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: In an eye-tracking study of 104 people reading Wikipedia, readability rose with font size and comprehension was better at 18 and 26 pt; the authors recommend 18 pt or larger for text-heavy sites.
evidence.source: Rello, Pielot & Marcos 2016, Make it big! The effect of font size and line spacing on online readability
evidence.authors: Rello L, Pielot M, Marcos MC
evidence.method: eye-tracking experiment, font sizes 10-26 pt, line spacing 0.8-1.8
evidence.quote_or_number: text-heavy websites should use fonts of size 18 or larger and use default line spacing

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: A review of on-screen text layout research found the number of characters per line is the key variable for line length.
evidence.source: Dyson 2004, How physical text layout affects reading from screen
evidence.quote_or_number: identifies the number of characters per line as the critical variable in looking at line length

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Older adults found 14-point fonts more legible than 12-point and preferred them.
evidence.source: Bernard, Liao & Mills 2001, The effects of font type and size on the legibility and reading time of online text by older adults
evidence.authors: Bernard ML, Liao CH, Mills M
evidence.method: lab experiment, 2 serif and 2 sans fonts at 12 and 14 pt
evidence.quote_or_number: participants significantly preferred the 14-point to the 12-point font size

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: Text-background colour pairs with higher contrast ratio were generally more readable.
evidence.source: Hall & Hanna 2004, The impact of web page text-background colour combinations on readability, retention, aesthetics and behavioural intention
evidence.quote_or_number: Colours with greater contrast ratio generally lead to greater readability

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: A major review of colour psychology warns that the field is young and that strong recommendations for practice are not yet warranted.
evidence.source: Elliot & Maier 2014, Color psychology: effects of perceiving color on psychological functioning in humans
evidence.method: narrative review of theory and experiments
evidence.quote_or_number: considerable work on boundary conditions, moderators, and real-world generalizability is needed before strong conceptual statements and recommendations for application are warranted

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: People like colours associated with things they like (blues with sky and clean water) and dislike colours tied to unpleasant things (browns with rot): colour preference is learned association.
evidence.source: Palmer & Schloss 2010, An ecological valence theory of human color preference
evidence.method: preference ratings plus object-association ratings, model fit
evidence.quote_or_number: People like colors strongly associated with objects they like (e.g., blues with clear skies and clean water) and dislike colors strongly associated with objects they dislike (e.g., browns with feces and rotten food).

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: On 20 news pages, white-space preferences differed by age, education and other traits; nobody preferred very high (90%) or very low (50%) white-space ratios.
evidence.source: Ko & Liu 2019, Old and young users' white space preferences for online news web pages
evidence.sample_size: survey sample (count not in abstract), 20 pages from 10 Chinese and English news sites
evidence.method: rating survey with SUS and VisAWI items
evidence.quote_or_number: None prefer too high (90%) or too low (50%) white-space ratio.

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: In 1,333 street observations of phone use (780 touching the screen), 49% held the phone in one hand, 36% cradled it in one hand and tapped with the other, and 15% used two hands.
evidence.source: Hoober 2013, How do users really hold mobile devices? (UXmatters)
evidence.method: field observation in public places over two months
evidence.quote_or_number: one handed -49% cradled -36% two handed -15%

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: The screen area a gripping thumb can reach depends on screen size, hand size and where the index finger rests behind the phone, and can be predicted with a model (fit on 20 people).
evidence.source: Bergström-Lehtovirta & Oulasvirta 2014, Modeling the functional area of the thumb on mobile touchscreen surfaces
evidence.method: motion capture of thumb trajectories, kinematic model
evidence.quote_or_number: The model predicts the functional area for a given 1) surface size, 2) hand size, and 3) position of the index finger on the back of the device.

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: For one-handed thumb use, targets of about 9.2 mm (single taps) and 9.6 mm (tap sequences) were large enough without hurting speed, errors or preference.
evidence.source: Parhi, Karlson & Bederson 2006, Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices
evidence.authors: Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB
evidence.sample_size: two-phase lab study (count not in abstract)
evidence.method: lab experiment, target sizes x screen positions
evidence.quote_or_number: target size of 9.2 mm for discrete tasks and targets of 9.6 mm for serial tasks should be sufficiently large for one-handed thumb use on touchscreen-based handhelds without degrading performance and preference

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: NN/g's rule from this research: interactive elements should be at least 1 cm x 1 cm, with enough spacing, to avoid slow taps and fat-finger errors.
evidence.source: Harley 2019, Touch targets on touchscreens (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.method: expert guidance based on Parhi et al. 2006
evidence.quote_or_number: Interactive elements must be at least 1cm x 1cm (0.4in x 0.4in) to support adequate selection time and prevent fat-finger errors.

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: On the move, people's attention to a phone breaks into bursts of a few seconds, versus spans of over 16 seconds in the lab.
evidence.source: Oulasvirta, Tamminen, Roto & Kuorelahti 2005, Interaction in 4-second bursts: the fragmented nature of attentional resources in mobile HCI
evidence.authors: Oulasvirta A, Tamminen S, Roto V, Kuorelahti J
evidence.sample_size: semi-naturalistic field study (count not in abstract), nine urban situations
evidence.method: field study measuring attention during mobile web tasks
evidence.quote_or_number: from spans of over 16 seconds in a laboratory condition dropping to bursts of just a few seconds in difficult mobile situations

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: In a quantitative study (179 users, 6 sites), people on desktop used hidden (hamburger) navigation in only 27% of cases versus 48-50% for visible or combined navigation.
evidence.source: Pernice & Budiu 2016, Hamburger menus and hidden navigation hurt UX metrics (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.method: quantitative remote usability test, mixed-effects regression
evidence.quote_or_number: On desktop, people used the hidden menus in only 27% of the cases, while they used visible or combo navigation almost twice as much: in 48% and 50% of the cases, respectively.

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: Hidden navigation also made tasks slower: at least 39% slower on desktop and 15% slower on phones (versus combined navigation).
evidence.source: Pernice & Budiu 2016, Hamburger menus and hidden navigation hurt UX metrics (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: people were at least 39% slower when the navigation was hidden

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: In NN/g eyetracking (120 people, 130,000+ fixations on long pages), 57% of viewing time was above the fold and 74% within the first two screenfuls.
evidence.source: Fessenden 2018, Scrolling and attention (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: In our most recent study, users spent about 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold.

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.5.8 (AA) requires pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing around smaller ones.
evidence.source: W3C 2023, Understanding SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (WCAG 2.2)
evidence.quote_or_number: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Robinhood users trade more on attention (top movers, hot stocks) than other retail investors; their intense buying predicts negative returns of -4.7% over 20 days for the most-bought stocks.
evidence.source: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz 2022, Attention-induced trading and returns: evidence from Robinhood users
evidence.authors: Barber BM, Huang X, Odean T, Schwarz C
evidence.sample_size: Robinhood holdings and trading data (large sample), with Robinhood outages as natural experiments
evidence.method: observational finance study with outage natural experiments
evidence.quote_or_number: Average 20-day abnormal returns are -4.7% (-19.6%) for the top stocks purchased each day (extreme herding events).

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: The same paper attributes part of Robinhood users' attention-driven trading to the app's own features, not only to the users it attracts.
evidence.source: Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz 2022, Attention-induced trading and returns: evidence from Robinhood users
evidence.authors: Barber BM, Huang X, Odean T, Schwarz C
evidence.quote_or_number: However, we show that it can also be partially driven by the app's unique features.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: In a randomised online experiment, hedonic gamification (confetti, badges) raised trading volume by 5.17%, and people with lower financial literacy preferred the gamified platforms.
evidence.source: Chapkovski, Khapko & Zoican 2024, Trading gamification and investor behavior
evidence.authors: Chapkovski P, Khapko M, Zoican M
evidence.sample_size: randomized online experiment (count not in abstract)
evidence.method: randomized online trading experiment with platform choice
evidence.quote_or_number: On average, hedonic gamification increases trading volume by 5.17%.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Participants with lower financial literacy chose platforms with hedonic gamification such as confetti and achievement badges.
evidence.source: Chapkovski, Khapko & Zoican 2024, Trading gamification and investor behavior
evidence.authors: Chapkovski P, Khapko M, Zoican M
evidence.quote_or_number: Participants with lower financial literacy prefer platforms with hedonic gamification elements, such as confetti and achievement badges.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Price-trend notifications helped investors with accurate beliefs learn but reinforced the mistakes of those with wrong beliefs.
evidence.source: Chapkovski, Khapko & Zoican 2024, Trading gamification and investor behavior
evidence.authors: Chapkovski P, Khapko M, Zoican M
evidence.quote_or_number: price trend notifications enhance learning for investors with accurate beliefs, but they reinforce trading mistakes for those with incorrect beliefs

evidence.question: Q6
evidence.claim: Comparing trades by the same investors across devices, smartphones increased buying of riskier, lottery-like assets and chasing past returns; the effect was not caused by screen size or nudges and did not fade.
evidence.source: Kalda, Loos, Previtero & Hackethal 2021, Smart(phone) investing? A within investor-time analysis of new technologies and trading behavior
evidence.authors: Kalda A, Loos B, Previtero A, Hackethal A
evidence.sample_size: transaction-level data from two German banks
evidence.quote_or_number: we find that smartphones increase purchasing of riskier and lottery-type assets and chasing past returns

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Instructional techniques that help inexperienced learners can lose their benefit and even hurt more experienced ones (the expertise reversal effect).
evidence.source: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller 2003, The expertise reversal effect
evidence.authors: Kalyuga S, Ayres P, Chandler P, Sweller J
evidence.quote_or_number: Instructional techniques that are highly effective with inexperienced learners can lose their effectiveness and even have negative consequences when used with more experienced learners.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Reformatting dense spacecraft displays gave large speed and accuracy gains for non-experts, while experts got fewer errors but no speed change.
evidence.source: Burns, Warren & Rudisill 1986, Formatting space-related displays to optimize expert and nonexpert user performance
evidence.authors: Burns MJ, Warren DL, Rudisill M
evidence.sample_size: experts and non-experts (count not in abstract)
evidence.method: lab experiment, two search tasks on original vs reformatted displays
evidence.quote_or_number: Large improvements in speed and accuracy were found for nonexperts on the reformatted displays. Experts had fewer errors but no response time difference on the reformatted displays.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Expert shortcuts are often left unused: people tend to stay with slower methods they already know, so interfaces must actively support the novice-to-expert transition.
evidence.source: Cockburn, Gutwin, Scarr & Malacria 2014, Supporting novice to expert transitions in user interfaces
evidence.authors: Cockburn A, Gutwin C, Scarr J, Malacria S
evidence.quote_or_number: research shows that many expert interface components are seldom used and that there is a tendency for users to persistently fail to adopt faster methods for completing their work

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: A meta-analysis of 33 samples (2,924 learners) found that friendly faces and pleasant colours in learning graphics improved retention, comprehension and transfer (d about 0.3-0.4).
evidence.source: Brom, Stárková & D'Mello 2018, How effective is emotional design? A meta-analysis on facial anthropomorphisms and pleasant colors during multimedia learning
evidence.authors: Brom C, Stárková T, D'Mello SK
evidence.quote_or_number: We found significant positive meta-analytic effects for retention (k = 18, d+ = 0.387), comprehension (k = 14, d+ = 0.317), and transfer (k = 27, d+ = 0.327) under a random-effects model.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: In that meta-analysis the warm design raised intrinsic motivation more for children than for older learners, and only weakly raised liking.
evidence.source: Brom, Stárková & D'Mello 2018, How effective is emotional design?
evidence.authors: Brom C, Stárková T, D'Mello SK
evidence.quote_or_number: There was provisional evidence that age moderated the effect of the manipulations on intrinsic motivation, such that larger effects were revealed for children compared to older learners.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: A systematic review of 73 studies on health websites found consensus that design, clear layout, interactive features and the owner's authority raise trust, while advertising lowers it.
evidence.source: Sbaffi & Rowley 2017, Trust and credibility in web-based health information: a review and agenda for future research
evidence.quote_or_number: There is a consensus that website design, clear layout, interactive features, and the authority of the owner have a positive effect on trust or credibility, whereas advertising has a negative effect.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: 18 guidelines for AI products (make clear what the AI can do and how well, support efficient correction, explain why) were validated with 49 designers testing 20 popular AI products.
evidence.source: Amershi et al. 2019, Guidelines for human-AI interaction
evidence.authors: Amershi S, Weld D, Vorvoreanu M, Fourney A, Nushi B, Collisson P, Suh J, Iqbal S, et al.
evidence.quote_or_number: These guidelines are validated through multiple rounds of evaluation including a user study with 49 design practitioners who tested the guidelines against 20 popular AI-infused products.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Showing a confidence score helped people calibrate their trust in an AI model, but local explanations were problematic and calibration alone did not improve joint decisions.
evidence.source: Zhang, Liao & Bellamy 2020, Effect of confidence and explanation on accuracy and trust calibration in AI-assisted decision making
evidence.authors: Zhang Y, Liao QV, Bellamy RKE
evidence.sample_size: two human experiments (counts not in abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: we show that confidence score can help calibrate people's trust in an AI model, but trust calibration alone is not sufficient to improve AI-assisted decision making

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: In a survey of 120 YouTube users, autoplay and recommendations mainly reduced people's sense of agency, while playlists and search supported it.
evidence.source: Lukoff et al. 2021, How the design of YouTube influences user sense of agency
evidence.authors: Lukoff K, Lyngs U, Zade H, Liao JV, Choi J, Fan K, Munson SA, Hiniker A
evidence.quote_or_number: From a survey of 120 U.S. users, we find that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermine sense of agency, while playlists and search support it.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: From the same data, NN/g estimates people read at most 28% of the words on an average web page, more likely about 20%.
evidence.source: Nielsen 2008, How little do users read? (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.venue: Nielsen Norman Group article (analysis of Weinreich et al. data)
evidence.quote_or_number: On the average Web page, users have time to read at most 28% of the words during an average visit; 20% is more likely.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Eyetracking shows people often scan text-heavy pages in an F shape, which is bad for users and businesses; good formatting (headings, bullets, bolded keywords) prevents it.
evidence.source: Pernice 2017 (reviewed 2026), F-shaped pattern of reading on the web: misunderstood, but still relevant (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: NN/g eyetracking studies (e.g. heatmap of 45+ people)
evidence.quote_or_number: The F-pattern is negative for users and businesses. Good design can prevent F-shape scanning .

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: A systematic review of 144 dashboards found eight groups of design patterns and distinct genres (narrative, analytical, embedded), each with trade-offs in screen space, interaction and information shown.
evidence.source: Bach et al. 2022, Dashboard design patterns
evidence.authors: Bach B, Freeman E, Abdul-Rahman A, Turkay C, Khan S, Fan Y, Chen M
evidence.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (VIS 2022)
evidence.quote_or_number: Based on a systematic review of 144 dashboards, we report on eight groups of design patterns that provide common solutions in dashboard design.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Dashboards differ widely in goals, interaction and practice, so 'dashboard' is not one design problem; the authors build a design space of dashboard types.
evidence.source: Sarikaya, Correll, Bartram, Tory & Fisher 2019, What do we talk about when we talk about dashboards?
evidence.authors: Sarikaya A, Correll M, Bartram L, Tory M, Fisher D
evidence.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (VIS 2018)
evidence.sample_size: analysis of dashboard examples and literature
evidence.quote_or_number: We characterize dashboards by their design goals, levels of interaction, and the practices around them.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Applying 20 form-design guidelines to real company forms led to faster completion, fewer submission attempts, fewer eye movements and higher satisfaction (eyetracking experiment, N = 65).
evidence.source: Seckler, Heinz, Bargas-Avila, Opwis & Tuch 2014, Designing usable web forms: empirical evaluation of web form improvement guidelines
evidence.authors: Seckler M, Heinz S, Bargas-Avila JA, Opwis K, Tuch AN
evidence.quote_or_number: Results indicate that improved web forms lead to faster completion times, fewer form submission trials, and fewer eye movements.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Baymard's survey of US shoppers: after excluding 'just browsing', 40% abandoned over extra costs, 19% over not trusting the site with their card, 18% over forced account creation and 17% over a long or complicated checkout.
evidence.source: Baymard Institute 2025-26, Cart abandonment rate statistics
evidence.venue: Baymard Institute research (quantitative survey and benchmark)
evidence.sample_size: quantitative survey of US online shoppers (n on Baymard's methodology page) plus 50 abandonment studies
evidence.method: survey and benchmark of checkout flows
evidence.quote_or_number: 40 % Extra costs too high (shipping, tax, fees) 20 % Delivery was too slow 19 % I didn't trust the site with my credit card information 18 % The site wanted me to create an account 17 % Too long / complicated checkout process

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Baymard's testing shows an ideal checkout needs only 12-14 form elements, yet the average US checkout shows 23.48 by default.
evidence.source: Baymard Institute 2025-26, Cart abandonment rate statistics
evidence.sample_size: large-scale checkout usability testing plus benchmark database
evidence.quote_or_number: the average US checkout flow contains 23.48 form elements displayed to users by default

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Teens dislike tiny font sizes as much as adults do, and nothing puts them off more than a cluttered screen full of text.
evidence.source: Kendrick & Nielsen 2019, Teenager's UX: designing for teens (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: teenagers dislike tiny font sizes as much as adults do

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: NN/g's research with children aged 3-12 found they need a different design style and content targeted narrowly by age, although much of what helps adults helps children too.
evidence.source: Sherwin & Nielsen 2019, Children's UX: usability issues in designing for young people (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: three study rounds with children 3-12 in the US and other countries
evidence.method: usability testing in lab and schools
evidence.quote_or_number: Designing for children requires distinct usability approaches, including targeting content narrowly for children of different ages.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: In NN/g testing, people's ability to use websites declined by about 0.8% a year between ages 25 and 60; older users are hurt by small text, low contrast and tiny targets.
evidence.source: Kane 2019, Usability for older adults: challenges and changes (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: 123 participants aged 65+ over three rounds (5 countries)
evidence.method: usability testing, focus groups, contextual inquiry
evidence.quote_or_number: between the ages of 25 and 60 people's ability to use websites declines by 0.8% per year

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: NN/g recommends skipping app onboarding where possible: its research on deck-of-cards tutorials found they did not improve task performance.
evidence.source: Kendrick 2020, Mobile-app onboarding: an analysis of components and techniques (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: our research on deck-of-cards tutorials, a method of instructional onboarding, showed that tutorials didn't improve task performance

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Empty states are a chance to show system status, teach the product and give a direct path to the key task.
evidence.source: Kaplan 2021, Designing empty states in complex applications: 3 guidelines (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Empty states provide opportunities for designers to communicate system status, increase learnability of the system, and deliver direct pathways for key tasks.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Data tables should support four tasks: find records, compare data, view or edit one row, and act on records; the first column should be a readable identifier and columns ordered by importance.
evidence.source: Laubheimer 2022, Data tables: four major user tasks (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: Table design should support four common user tasks: find records that fit specific criteria, compare data, view/edit/add a single row's data, and take actions on records.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: GOV.UK's design principles put accessibility above elegance: 'If we have to sacrifice elegance - so be it.'
evidence.source: Government Digital Service 2012 (updated 2019), Government design principles (GOV.UK)
evidence.quote_or_number: Accessible design is good design. Everything we build should be as inclusive, legible and readable as possible. If we have to sacrifice elegance - so be it.

evidence.question: Q2
evidence.claim: Removing the heads-up display in a shooter game increased immersion for expert players through more cognitive involvement and sense of control; the right interface depends on expertise.
evidence.source: Iacovides, Cox, Kennedy, Cairns & Jennett 2015, Removing the HUD: the impact of non-diegetic game elements and expertise on player involvement
evidence.authors: Iacovides I, Cox AL, Kennedy R, Cairns P, Jennett C
evidence.sample_size: lab study with two game versions (count not in abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: Our findings suggest that the removal of non-diegetic elements, such as the heads-up display, is able to influence immersion in expert players through increasing their cognitive involvement and sense of control.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: For online news, traditional credibility factors still matter and hyperlinking mattered for index-type sites, but multimedia and interactivity did not change credibility.
evidence.source: Chung, Nam & Stefanone 2012, Exploring online news credibility: the relative influence of traditional and technological factors
evidence.authors: Chung CJ, Nam Y, Stefanone MA
evidence.sample_size: survey of news readers (count not in abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: Multimediality and interactivity did not influence credibility perceptions.

evidence.question: Q3
evidence.claim: Luxury consumers are split on brand websites: some see e-commerce and interactive tools as a loss of prestige or exclusivity, and attitudes follow whether they buy luxury for themselves or to show others (42 interviews).
evidence.source: Veg-Sala & Geerts 2023, Consumers' expectations toward luxury brands' websites
evidence.quote_or_number: However, luxury consumers might still have different perceptions regarding these websites, as it can be seen as a loss of prestige or selectivity.

evidence.question: Q5
evidence.claim: White space in advertising carries a historically built meaning that both ad makers (creative directors) and ordinary consumers share and understand.
evidence.source: Pracejus, Olsen & O'Guinn 2006, How nothing became something: white space, rhetoric, history, and meaning
evidence.authors: Pracejus JW, Olsen GD, O'Guinn TC
evidence.sample_size: historical analysis plus interviews with creative directors and consumers
evidence.quote_or_number: how this meaning is today shared and understood by both producers of ads (ad agency creative directors) and the readers of ads (ordinary consumers)

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: Over two weeks of real use (60 mobile-phone users), the boost that an attractive design gave to perceived usability faded as people used it more.
evidence.source: Sonderegger, Zbinden, Uebelbacher & Sauer 2012, The influence of product aesthetics and usability over the course of time: a longitudinal field experiment
evidence.authors: Sonderegger A, Zbinden G, Uebelbacher A, Sauer J
evidence.sample_size: 60 mobile phone users, 3 sessions over 2 weeks
evidence.method: longitudinal field experiment, 2 x 2 x 3 mixed design
evidence.quote_or_number: A major finding was that the positive effect of an aesthetically appealing product on perceived usability, reported in many previous studies, began to wane with increasing exposure time.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: Because aesthetics sways usability ratings in one-off tests, the authors advise multi-session (longitudinal) usability tests.
evidence.source: Sonderegger, Zbinden, Uebelbacher & Sauer 2012, The influence of product aesthetics and usability over the course of time
evidence.authors: Sonderegger A, Zbinden G, Uebelbacher A, Sauer J
evidence.quote_or_number: When completing a usability test it is therefore advisable to adopt a longitudinal multiple-session approach to reduce the possibly undesirable influence of aesthetics on usability ratings.

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: The novelty effect (higher use right after launch) appears both when a new system arrives and again whenever an existing system is changed, so short trials overstate the appeal of anything new.
evidence.source: Koch, von Luck, Schwarzer & Draheim 2018, The novelty effect in large display deployments: experiences and lessons-learned for evaluating prototypes
evidence.authors: Koch M, von Luck K, Schwarzer J, Draheim S
evidence.venue: ECSCW 2018 (European Society for Socially Embedded Technologies)
evidence.sample_size: own field deployments plus literature review
