evidence.quote_or_number: We found that the novelty effect is prevalently present on two occasions: (a) immediately after a new system is deployed in a new environment, and (b) in reoccurring situations, when changes are made to an existing system.

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: Google reports well-applied expressive design was preferred across all ages, most strongly (up to 87%) by 18-24 year olds.
evidence.source: Google Design 2025, Expressive design: Google's UX research
evidence.quote_or_number: We found that well-applied, expressive design is strongly preferred by people of all ages, with that preference being particularly strong - up to 87% - among 18-to-24-year-olds.

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: In Google's eyetracking test of 10 apps, people found key controls up to four times faster in the expressive versions, mainly because primary actions were larger, coloured and placed near use.
evidence.source: Google Design 2025, Expressive design: Google's UX research
evidence.sample_size: lab eyetracking with a diverse group across 10 apps (count not given)
evidence.quote_or_number: Participants were able to spot key UI elements up to four times faster in the M3 Expressive designs

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: Google also found expressive concepts that broke familiar patterns (unlabelled icons, scattered album art instead of a list) looked modern but scored worse on usability, and unfamiliarity lowered results.
evidence.source: Google Design 2025, Expressive design: Google's UX research
evidence.quote_or_number: While users reported the interface looked modern and exciting, usability scores suffered.

evidence.question: Q8
evidence.claim: A design leader argued that Dribbble-style showcase work rewards surface polish: much of it looks the same across product types and ignores real problems.
evidence.source: Adams 2014, The dribbblisation of design (Intercom blog)
evidence.quote_or_number: A huge majority of the product design work on Dribbble looks the same.

evidence.question: Q9
evidence.claim: Feature Congestion, a computational measure of visual clutter that works on any screenshot, is a widely used stand-in for how hard a display is to search.
evidence.source: Rosenholtz, Li & Nakano 2007, Measuring visual clutter
evidence.authors: Rosenholtz R, Li Y, Nakano L
evidence.quote_or_number: This Feature Congestion measure of visual clutter is based on the analogy that the more cluttered a display or scene is, the more difficult it would be to add a new item that would reliably draw attention.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: Ten years of SUS data across many products showed the scale is robust and versatile, and the authors added an adjective rating and guidance on what counts as an acceptable score.
evidence.source: Bangor, Kortum & Miller 2008, An empirical evaluation of the System Usability Scale
evidence.authors: Bangor A, Kortum PT, Miller JT
evidence.sample_size: nearly 10 years of SUS data from many products
evidence.method: analysis of a large SUS dataset
evidence.quote_or_number: Results from the analysis of this large number of SUS scores show that the SUS is a highly robust and versatile tool for usability professionals.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: Across 11 studies, usability problem discovery follows a Poisson model; for a medium project the best benefit-to-cost ratio came at about four evaluators or users.
evidence.source: Nielsen & Landauer 1993, A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems
evidence.quote_or_number: For a "medium" example, we estimate that 16 evaluations would be worth their cost, with maximum benefit/cost ratio at four.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: NN/g's rule: five users find about 85% of a design's usability problems; three small rounds of five beat one study of fifteen, while quantitative studies need about 20 users.
evidence.source: Nielsen 2000, Why you only need to test with 5 users (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.quote_or_number: The ultimate user experience is improved much more by 3 studies with 5 users each than by a single monster study with 15 users.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: The Microsoft Desirability Toolkit (product reaction cards) has people pick the five words, from 118, that best describe a design; NN/g recommends cutting the list to about 25 for online surveys of visual appeal.
evidence.source: Moran 2016, Using the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit to test visual appeal (Nielsen Norman Group)
evidence.sample_size: n/a (method; original Benedek & Miner 2002 at Microsoft)
evidence.quote_or_number: They created 118 physical cards with different product-reaction words written on each card. At the end of usability testing sessions, participants were given the deck of cards and asked to select the five words that best described the product.

evidence.question: Q10
evidence.claim: When first clicks went down the right path, 87% of users eventually succeeded at the task; after a wrong first click only 46% did.
evidence.source: Sauro 2011, Getting the first click right (MeasuringU)
evidence.quote_or_number: Research has shown that when users' first click is down the right path, 87% eventually succeed. When they click down an incorrect path, only 46% eventually succeed.
